topic.title: Cumulative frequency tables and curves; estimating median, quartiles and IQR
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One of the last five questions on almost every M3 paper, 5 to 6 marks in three parts: complete the cumulative frequency column (1), draw the curve (2 to 3), then read something off it (2). The reading part alternates between the median and interquartile range and a count between or above given values. The same statement is examined again in M4, M7 and M8.
mustMemorise: Plot each running total at the UPPER class boundary, never the midpoint or the lower bound
Join the points with one smooth curve; a bar chart scores nothing and kills the follow-through
Median at n ÷ 2 on the cumulative frequency axis, quartiles at n ÷ 4 and 3n ÷ 4; read across, then down
Number above a value = total − reading; number between two values = the difference of the two readings
Answer in the units of the axis: a reading on an axis marked in £1000s is not a number of pounds
notOnThisSpec: Cumulative frequency step polygons for discrete data: CCEA draws the curve for grouped continuous data
Standard deviation: the specification names only the range and the interquartile range as measures of spread
Percentiles and deciles: only the median and the two quartiles are read from the curve
Any formula for the median of grouped data: CCEA expects the reading to come off the graph

mustBeAbleTo: Turn a grouped frequency column into a cumulative frequency column of running totals
Say which value of the variable each running total is plotted against, and why it is the upper class boundary
Plot the points on a printed grid and join them with one smooth curve
Read the median by going across from n ÷ 2 on the cumulative frequency axis and down to the variable axis
Read both quartiles from n ÷ 4 and 3n ÷ 4 and subtract them for the interquartile range
Commit to a reading that falls between grid lines
Estimate how many values are above a given value, below it, or between two values
Convert a reading into the units the question asks for, including an axis marked in thousands
Compare two distributions with one sentence about the medians and one about the spread
sheet.howExamined: A five or six mark question near the end of the M3 paper. Part (a) completes the cumulative frequency column and is almost always answered well. Part (b) draws the curve on a printed grid, worth 2 or 3 marks, with the plotting mark lost if the points sit at midpoints or lower bounds. Part (c) reads the graph: the median and interquartile range, or a count between two values, or a count above a value, for 2 marks with follow-through from the candidate's own curve. The same question shape appears in M4, M7 and M8.
traps: Points plotted at the class midpoint or the lower bound: in Summer 2025 M3 Q24(b) all three positions appeared in roughly equal numbers, and only the upper bound scored
A bar chart instead of a curve: no marks in that part and no follow-through in the next (November 2024 M4 Q13)
The median read as the halfway point of the horizontal axis instead of n ÷ 2 on the vertical axis (Summer 2024 M3 Q26(a)(i))
Refusing to give a reading that is not on a grid line, when the examiners say a value in between is exactly what is wanted (Summer 2024 M4 Q10(a)(i))
The interquartile range not attempted at all, or measured from the median to one quartile (Summer 2024 M3 Q26(a)(ii))
Readings on an axis marked in £1000s written as pounds without multiplying by 1000 (Summer 2025 M3 Q24(c) and M4 Q11(c))
A count between two values given as one reading instead of the difference of two (November 2024 M3 Q27(c))

workedExamples.stem:
The table shows the masses, $m$ grams, of 80 eggs graded at a farm.

| Mass ($m$ g) | $40 < m \le 45$ | $45 < m \le 50$ | $50 < m \le 55$ | $55 < m \le 60$ | $60 < m \le 65$ | $65 < m \le 70$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 5 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 11 | 4 |

Complete a cumulative frequency column, draw the cumulative frequency curve and use it to estimate the median mass. [4]

data.caption: The masses of 80 eggs graded at a farm; the cumulative frequency column is started for you

steps.decision: Each entry is the total so far, not the class on its own. The last entry must equal the number of eggs, which is a free check that the column is right.

Every running total is plotted at the UPPER boundary of its class. At $m = 50$ the total of 25 is only complete once the whole class up to 50 g has been counted, so 25 belongs above 50, not above the midpoint 47.5.

options: Because the running total is only complete at the top of the class
Because the midpoint is used for the mean, so the upper bound must be used here to be different
Because the upper bound is always a whole number
whyMenu.explain: A cumulative frequency answers the question how many are this value or less, and that question is only answered once the whole class has been counted, at its upper boundary.

steps.working: Join the seven points, in order, with one smooth curve.
steps.decision: A curve, never bars. A bar chart earns nothing here and, in November 2024, also lost the follow-through marks in the part that read the graph.

steps.working: $n = 80$, so read across from $\tfrac{80}{2} = 40$ on the cumulative frequency axis, then straight down: about $53.75$ g.
steps.decision: Half of 80 is 40, and 40 is a height on the vertical axis. The halfway point of the mass axis, 55 g, has nothing to do with the median.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Cumulative frequencies 5, 25, 45, 65, 76, 80; curve through the upper class boundaries; median about 53.75 g.

workedExamples.stem:
The curve shows the lengths, $L$ cm, of 60 courgettes picked from an allotment.

Use the graph to estimate how many of the courgettes were longer than 20 cm. [2]

figure.alt: A cumulative frequency curve for the lengths of 60 courgettes, through (10, 0), (14, 4), (18, 16), (22, 40), (26, 54) and (30, 60). The horizontal axis runs from 10 to 30 cm in steps of 4 with small squares of 1 cm; the vertical axis runs from 0 to 60 in steps of 10.

steps.working: Find 20 on the length axis and go straight up to the curve, then across to the cumulative frequency axis.
steps.decision: The curve always answers how many are this value or less. So the first reading is the number of courgettes 20 cm or shorter, not the number the question wants.

options: Because a cumulative frequency counts everything up to that value
Because the curve is increasing, so reading up always gives the larger group
Because 20 cm is not a class boundary
whyMenu.explain: Every point on the curve is a running total, so the height above 20 cm is the number at 20 cm or less.

steps.working: The reading at $20$ cm is about $28$.
steps.decision: Commit to the reading even though it is not on a grid line. Examiners say a value in between is exactly what they expect.
Subtract from the total, because the curve counted the wrong end. The answer is a number of courgettes, so it is a whole number.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: About 32 courgettes were longer than 20 cm.

workedExamples.stem:
The curve shows the values, $V$, of 100 cars at a dealership. $V$ is measured in thousands of pounds.

Use the graph to estimate the interquartile range of the values. Give your answer in pounds. [3]

figure.alt: The cumulative frequency curve for the values of 100 cars, with dashed lines across from 25 down to about 9 and across from 75 down to about 18 on an axis marked in thousands of pounds.

steps.working: $n = 100$, so the quartiles are read across from $\tfrac{100}{4} = 25$ and $\tfrac{3 \times 100}{4} = 75$.
steps.decision: Both starting points are on the cumulative frequency axis. A quarter of the way along the value axis would be £7500, which has nothing to do with the quartile.

steps.working: Lower quartile about $9$; upper quartile about $18$. IQR on the axis $= 18 - 9 = 9$.
steps.decision: Write both quartiles down before subtracting, so the reading mark is visible even if the subtraction slips.

steps.working: The axis is in £1000s, so the interquartile range is $9 \times 1000 = £9000$.
steps.decision: Read the axis label before writing the answer line. In Summer 2025 many candidates lost this mark by leaving the answer in thousands.

options: Because the axis is labelled in thousands of pounds and the question asks for pounds
Because an interquartile range is always larger than the reading
Because money answers are always multiplied by 1000
whyMenu.explain: The number on the axis is a count of thousands; the question asks for pounds, so the unit has to be converted.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Interquartile range about £9000 (9 on an axis marked in £1000s).

items.stem: A cumulative frequency graph is drawn for the class $20 < t \le 30$, whose running total is 47. Where does the point go?
items.skill: Plot a running total at the upper class boundary

options.feedback: Yes. The total of 47 counts everything up to 30, so it belongs at the upper class boundary.
25 is the class midpoint, which belongs to an estimated mean. In Summer 2025 this cost a mark on both M3 and M4.
At $t = 20$ none of this class has been counted, so the total of 47 is not reached yet.
The class width is used for frequency density in a histogram, not for the position of a cumulative point.

items.stem: In a cumulative frequency table the frequencies are 7, 11, 18, 9 and 5. What is the third cumulative frequency?
items.skill: Build the running totals of a cumulative frequency column

options.feedback: 18 is that class's own frequency. A cumulative frequency adds every class up to it.
50 is the total of all five classes, which is the last entry of the column, not the third.
That is the total of the classes after this one. Running totals build from the top down.

items.stem: A cumulative frequency curve is drawn for 90 people. Where do you start to estimate the median?
items.skill: Find the median from a curve

options.text: At 45 on the cumulative frequency axis, then across to the curve
options.feedback: Yes: $90 \div 2 = 45$, read across, then down.

options.text: Halfway along the horizontal axis, then up to the curve
options.feedback: In Summer 2024 M3 Q26 too many did exactly this. The median halves the people, not the axis.

options.text: At 90 on the cumulative frequency axis
options.feedback: 90 is everybody. The median is the halfway height, 45.

options.text: At the steepest part of the curve
options.feedback: The steepest part shows the most crowded class, which is about the mode, not the median.

items.stem: A cumulative frequency curve is drawn for 64 values. At what cumulative frequency do you read across for the upper quartile?
items.skill: Find the quartile positions on a cumulative frequency axis

options.feedback: Yes: $\tfrac{3 \times 64}{4} = 48$.
32 is $\tfrac{n}{2}$, which gives the median. The upper quartile is three quarters of the way up.
16 is $\tfrac{n}{4}$, the lower quartile.

options.text: Three quarters of the way along the horizontal axis
options.feedback: Quartiles are quarters of the data, so they are counted up the cumulative frequency axis.

items.stem: A cumulative frequency graph for 200 shoppers gives a reading of 138 at £40. How many shoppers spent more than £40?
items.skill: Count above a value from a cumulative reading

options.feedback: Yes: $200 - 138 = 62$. The curve counts downwards, so subtract from the total.
138 is the number who spent £40 or less. Subtract it from 200.
Half of the shoppers is the median group, not the number above £40.
That is $200 - 40$, mixing the money axis with the cumulative frequency axis.

items.stem: A median read from a curve falls between two grid lines, at about 12.4. What should you write?
items.skill: Commit to a reading between grid lines

options.feedback: Yes. Summer 2024 M4 Q10 says plainly that a value between grid lines is completely acceptable.
Moving to the nearest grid line throws away the accuracy the scheme is looking for.
There is no rule that readings land on halves. Read what the graph shows.

options.text: Nothing, because the median cannot be read here
options.feedback: A blank scores nothing. An estimate from your own curve is what the question asks for.

items.stem: On a curve whose horizontal axis is marked Price (£1000s), the quartiles read 155 and 245. What is the interquartile range?
items.skill: Convert a reading on an axis marked in thousands

options.feedback: Yes: $245 - 155 = 90$ on the axis, and the axis is in thousands, so £90 000.
The subtraction is right but the axis label was missed. Summer 2025 M3 Q24(c) turned on exactly this.
The quartiles are subtracted, not added, to give the interquartile range.
That is the upper quartile on its own. The interquartile range is the gap between the two quartiles.

items.stem: A curve for 50 journeys reads 12 at 24 minutes and 43 at 38 minutes. How many journeys took between 24 and 38 minutes?
items.skill: Count between two values from two readings

options.feedback: Yes: $43 - 12 = 31$. Between two values is the difference of the two readings.
43 counts every journey of 38 minutes or less, including the short ones. Subtract the reading at 24 minutes.
$50 - 43 = 7$ counts the journeys longer than 38 minutes, not those in between.
$38 - 24 = 14$ subtracts the two times, not the two cumulative readings.

A cumulative frequency graph is being drawn for the class $50 < m \le 55$.

Write down the value of $m$ at which the point for this class is plotted.

scheme.for: 55, the upper class boundary

hints: The running total counts everything up to the top of the class.
So the point sits above the largest mass the class can contain.
parts.workedSolution: The cumulative frequency counts every egg of mass 55 g or less, so the point belongs at the upper class boundary, $m = 55$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the class midpoint, which is used for an estimated mean, not for a cumulative frequency graph. The running total is only complete at the top of the class.

A cumulative frequency diagram is never bars.

figures.alt: A cumulative frequency curve for the masses of 80 eggs. The curve passes through (40, 0), (45, 5), (50, 25), (55, 45), (60, 65), (65, 76) and (70, 80). parts.stem: Use the graph to estimate the median mass of an egg.

scheme.for: median read as 53.75 g (accept 53.25 to 54.25)

hints: There are 80 eggs, so read across from $\tfrac{80}{2} = 40$ on the cumulative frequency axis.
Go across to the curve, then straight down to the mass axis.
parts.workedSolution: $n = 80$, so read across from 40 on the vertical axis. The curve is met above about $53.75$ g, so the median mass is about $53.75$ g.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the halfway point of the mass axis, not the halfway point of the data. Halve the number of eggs and read across from the cumulative frequency axis.
That reading comes from a curve drawn through the class midpoints. Each running total belongs at the top of its class, so the curve sits further to the right.

parts.stem: Use the graph to estimate the interquartile range of the masses.

scheme.for: both quartiles read from the curve: 48.75 (accept 48.25 to 49.25) and 58.75 (accept 58.25 to 59.25)
subtraction giving 10 g (accept 9 to 11)

hints: Read across from $\tfrac{80}{4} = 20$ for the lower quartile and from $\tfrac{3 \times 80}{4} = 60$ for the upper quartile.
Interquartile range = upper quartile − lower quartile.
parts.workedSolution:
Lower quartile: read across from 20, giving about $48.75$ g. Upper quartile: read across from 60, giving about $58.75$ g.

IQR $\approx 58.75 - 48.75 = 10$ g.

commonErrors.feedback: You measured from the median up to the upper quartile. The interquartile range runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile.
That is the width of the whole mass axis. The interquartile range is the gap between two readings taken from the curve.

context.setting: Daily rainfall recorded at a weather station over 80 days

figures.alt: A cumulative frequency curve for the daily rainfall on 80 days, through (0, 0), (10, 12), (20, 40), (30, 60), (40, 74) and (50, 80). The horizontal axis runs from 0 to 50 mm in steps of 10 with small squares of 2 mm; the vertical axis runs from 0 to 80 in steps of 10.

parts.stem:
The curve shows the daily rainfall, $r$ mm, recorded at a weather station on 80 days.

Use the graph to estimate the median daily rainfall.

scheme.for: median read as 20 mm (accept 19 to 21)

hints: Read across from $\tfrac{80}{2} = 40$ on the cumulative frequency axis.
parts.workedSolution: Read across from 40 and down: the median is about $20$ mm.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the middle of the rainfall axis. The median splits the 80 days in half, so start at 40 on the vertical axis.

parts.stem: Use the graph to estimate the number of days on which more than 24 mm of rain fell.

scheme.for: reading at 24 mm of about 48 seen

hints: Read up from 24 mm to the curve.
The curve counts days with 24 mm or less, so subtract from 80.
parts.workedSolution: At $24$ mm the cumulative frequency is about $48$ days. More than 24 mm: $80 - 48 = 32$ days.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the number of days with 24 mm or less. Subtract it from the 80 days to count the wetter days.

The curve shows the lifetimes, $h$ hours, of 80 batteries.

findings.asked: Median and interquartile range from a cumulative frequency curve, then compare with another data set.
findings.wentWrong: Too many gave the median as the halfway point on the horizontal axis (12.5) instead of halving the total on the vertical axis; the IQR was unfamiliar; comparisons quoted values without meaning.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Read across from n/2 and down; found UQ - LQ; compared with sentences such as 'greater median so longer delays on average' and 'greater spread so less consistent'.
findings.rule: Median: n/2 on the cumulative axis, across, then down.

findings.asked: Median and IQR from a curve; compare with a box plot.
findings.wentWrong: Candidates would not commit to a reading between grid lines; the IQR was often 7 by generous tolerance; for comparisons most said one median was higher but few used 'spread' or 'variation' for the IQR.
findings.rule: Readings between grid lines are expected; describe an IQR difference as spread.

findings.asked: Complete a cumulative frequency table, draw the curve, estimate a count between two times.
findings.wentWrong: Table and curve mostly right; a bar chart scored nothing and forfeited follow-through; the final estimate suffered from misread times.
findings.rule: A cumulative frequency graph is a curve through the points, never bars.

findings.wentWrong: Curves were plotted at upper bounds, midpoints and lower bounds in roughly equal numbers; in the IQR many forgot the readings were in thousands.
findings.rule: Plot at the upper class boundary; answer in the units of the axis.

findings.wentWrong: Mostly right; plotting at lower bounds or midpoints cost a mark; the IQR lost the thousands or was read inaccurately.
findings.rule: Upper boundaries, smooth curve, careful reading with the scale.

findings.asked: Cumulative frequency, curve, then the number between two given times.
findings.wentWrong: Table and curve fine; only the best read the two times and subtracted.
findings.rule: Between two values = difference of the two cumulative readings.

insight.ruleToRemember: Plot at upper class boundaries and join smoothly; median at n/2 on the vertical axis; IQR = UQ - LQ in the axis units; compare with one average sentence and one spread sentence.
insight.aStarSignal: Confident readings off grid lines, an IQR in the right units, and a comparison that says what the median and IQR mean in the context.
